blocks.x: Pocket-sized Hong Kong packs more of a punch than its 430-square-mile size might suggest. Split into three main areas—Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, and the New Territories—made up of 18 districts, each with their own rich history, culture, architecture, and foods, there's more than enough to keep the average tourist busy for months, never mind the usual weekend trip.

With more than seven million people packed into over 9,000 high-rises, efficiency is key here, and people will judge you for holding up lines, hesitating with your Octopus card, or lingering over your dim sum table while others are waiting. That said, Hong Kong people are generally kind and helpful when it comes to asking for directions. Most also speak English, which is one of the city’s official languages.
These are the unwritten rules of traveling to Hong Kong you should bookmark to seamlessly go with the flow on your next trip.

1. Grab an Octopus at the airport

An amped-up version of London's Oyster card, Hong Kong's contactless Octopus card makes getting around the city a breeze. Download the app for free or pick a physical card at the Airport Express ticket desk in the arrivals hall or any MTR subway station (the 50 Hong Kong Dollars (or around $6.50) deposit is refunded when you return the card). It can be used on every form of transport in the city, including the Peak Tram, regular trams and ferries to the Outlying Islands, such as Lamma and Cheung Chau, as well as at more than 30,000 retail outlets from convenience stores to fast food outlets, to cinemas and museums. Load up and go.
2. Use the buses

Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railways system, or MTR, covers large swathes of Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, and the New Territories, but it's the double-decker buses and pocket-rocket minibuses that fill in the gaps—often with fantastic views of the city along the way. Hop on the #6 double-decker from Central to Stanley beach, which lurches around Hong Kong Island's mountainous southern South China Sea coast (sit upstairs on the right-hand side). Or try the #94, which winds from Sai Kung Village through Hong Kong's lush UNESCO Global Geopark to Wong Shek Pier, where you can catch a scenic old wooden ferry (known as a kaito) back to Shatin to connect to the MTR line.

3. Master public transport etiquette

On the subject of public transport, there are certain rules which everyone follows. Keep right on any escalators or walkways, always let passengers alight before you board, and give you up your seat to anyone in need. And while it might be fine to crack open a bag of chips or slurp a coffee in the NYC subway, eating and drinking is not allowed on any trains, trams, buses, or ferries in Hong Kong—which is why they're all spotlessly clean.
4. Make the most of our museums

Hong Kong is such an outdoors-y destination that it can seem like there's little to do on a rainy day but the city has two wonderful world-class museums—the Hong Kong Palace Museum (70 Hong Kong Dollars, or around $9), which contains hundreds of priceless treasures borrowed from the Palace Museum in Beijing, and the gigantic M+ Museum (190 Hong Kong Dollars, or around $24.25), where the focus is highly visual contemporary Asian arts. Both should be on your list to visit rain or shine. On top of that, there are dozens of fascinating little niche museums, from a British colonial-era building dedicated to tea (Flagstaff House), to the Central Star Ferry's Maritime Museum, to The Mills, which celebrates the city's textiles industry—and almost all are free to visit on Wednesdays.

5. Tick the box for dim sum

Served from morning until early afternoon, dim sum is the fuel that Hong Kong runs on. To beat the crowds, it's best to arrive before 12 p.m. or after 2 p.m. (try one of the world's most affordable Michelin star restaurants, Tim Ho Wan, or the 90-year old Luk Yu Teahouse). In larger establishments you might be given your own table; in smaller joints you'll be squeezed onto a bench elbow to elbow with strangers. Tea is usually included and already on the table—tap the table with two fingers if you need a refill. Menus tend to be printed order forms with tiny photographs of each dish. Write in the amount of each dish that you desire and then wave the form in the air for a server to pick up. To pay, take your completed form to the cashier when you're leaving.
6. Please don't say “Ni hao”

The people of Hong Kong speak Cantonese, not Mandarin, which is spoken in mainland China. The colorful, highly expressive Cantonese language forms an essential part of the city's identity, so while it's unlikely that anyone will tell you off for a cheerful “Ni hao,” you will definitely earn eye rolls. The traditional greeting in Hong Kong—and Macau—is, “Jo sun” in the morning, and, “Nei ho” throughout the rest of the day. Another handy phrase worth memorizing is “Mmm goi” meaning excuse me and thank you.
